newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia must reform or face decline-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia must reform or face decline-analysts.

text.p: Slovenia, eager to defend its place among Europe's most prosperous reform states, has to grapple with tough economic reforms or risk falling behind, economic analysts said on Monday.

Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek and his centre-left Liberal Democrats, who emerged as the strongest party from Sunday's general election with 27.1 percent of the vote, was the best choice to do the job, they said.
"The basic course is clear and there's a national consensus about the course of economic policy," Igor Strmsnik of the government's Institute of Macroeconomic Analysis told Reuters.
"It's impossible to put off reforms. There is very little time left, and we simply don't have a second-best scenario."

Analysts agree that Slovenians will have to accept stagnant wages, cuts in welfare and even rising unemployment as the ex-Yugoslav republic tries to get in shape for membership in the European Union by the year 2001.

"If the Liberal Democrats stay in power, possibly in a coalition with the People's Party, it will make for a strong government that will have the power to do just that," said France Krizanic, an economist at Ljubljana University.
The rightist People's Party came second in the poll with 19.6 percent of the vote, and is widely seen as the most likely candidate to team up with the Liberal Democrats.

The People's Party leader Marjan Podobnik said an alliance of rightwing parties may team up to form the next government, which an analyst said would slow down the country's already sluggish privatisation and scare off foreign investors.
"If they form a government, foreign investment will stay in the doldrums," said Miha Kovac, a political analyst.

While Slovenia's economy grew by a comfortable 3.5 percent last year, and inflation is running at below 10 percent, the country is plagued by unemployment rates exceeding 13 percent. With the restructuring of the former command economy far from completed, this figure may well rise still.
"The main challenge is unemployment," said Krizanic.
But average tax rates are already at 36 percent and the government budget's share in national income is stretched to the limit, analysts say.

Key on the reform agenda will be a long-planned but repeatedly delayed overhaul of the pension system, covering about a fifth of the two million Slovenes. "Ther's more than 400,000 pensioners. They're important voters," said Krizanic.
The Alpine republic was hit by a wave of industrial action this year and the government gave in to many of the demands.

As a consequence, average wages were up 14.3 percent in the first eight months of the year, prompting widespread concern about rising inflation and declining competitiveness of Slovenia's strongly export-oriented industry.

"Slovenia now has to make the cuts that were impossible to make before the election," said Strmsnik. "The catch is that we'll have to freeze budget expenditures and secure economic growth at the same time."
Growth is expected to fall to three percent this year from as much as five percent in 1994, and independent analysts say next year's rate will hardly be more than two percent.
Yet while increasing the need for swift reforms, Slovenia's strong dependence on the EU economy may also present an opportunity to help the government do just that.

"We're very dependent on Europe and it now looks like the European economy is recovering," Strmsnik said. "If we have growth here then the reforms will be easier. If not, we'll have a political problem."
